hitl_conditions: Explicitly a 'human-in-the-loop DT system', not autonomous: humans evaluate and execute ML-suggested mitigation sets; role unchanged by real-time updates. Authors note workforce training, data infrastructure and weekly/event-triggered updates as implementation conditions (Sect. 3, 5).
key_finding: Simulated DT (Simio DES: five-station plant, five suppliers, (Q,r) inventory, condition-based maintenance) with six ML regressors as surrogates predicting profit of 5,880 mitigation combinations; static recommendations recover 72%/50% of lost profit (32/48-day delays), and real-time state updates at supply arrival change the optimal mix (forklift, reorder quantity, overtime).

quotes.text: The research in this article does not interface with data from a real manufacturing facility; however, the architecture and operation of the proposed model conform to the fundamental principles of a DT.
This necessitates the acquisition of five distinct materials from five suppliers. As shown in Table 2, the lead time in days for each supplier follows a gamma distribution.
This article presents a framework for using DT simulations integrated with predictive machine learning models to manage supply chain disruptions in manufacturing settings.

Linear regression was chosen for its simplicity and interpretability, functioning as a linear benchmark. To model nonlinear interactions and enhance predictive performance, we tested K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Decision Tree, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting regression models.

As described in Fig. 1, this DT functions as a real-time decision support tool, not as a closed-loop control system. The simulation-prediction framework offers suggestions for mitigating disruptions, which are presumed to be evaluated and executed by human decision makers.

The model simulates real-time system behavior but does not perform physical control actions directly. This design conceives of a human-in-the-loop DT system, as opposed to entirely autonomous cyber–physical systems.
